stem: Macroeconomics is the branch of economics that studies __________.
options: The economy as a whole — aggregates like national income, total output, general price level, employment and growth
The behaviour of a single consumer only
The pricing of one commodity in one market
The budget of a single household
solution: MACROECONOMICS studies the ECONOMY as a WHOLE — dealing with AGGREGATES such as NATIONAL INCOME, TOTAL OUTPUT and employment, the GENERAL PRICE LEVEL (inflation), aggregate demand and supply, and economic GROWTH. It contrasts with MICROECONOMICS, which studies individual units (a single consumer, firm, or market). So option 1 is correct.

stem: Microeconomics differs from macroeconomics in that microeconomics deals with __________.
options: Individual economic units — a particular consumer, firm, or the market for a single good
The total output of the whole country
The general price level of the economy
solution: MICROECONOMICS deals with INDIVIDUAL economic UNITS — a PARTICULAR CONSUMER, a particular FIRM, or the MARKET for a SINGLE GOOD — and how prices and quantities are determined for them. MACROECONOMICS, in contrast, deals with economy-wide aggregates. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The emergence of macroeconomics as a distinct branch is largely credited to __________.
options: John Maynard Keynes and his 1936 book 'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money'
solution: The emergence of MACROECONOMICS as a distinct branch is largely credited to JOHN MAYNARD KEYNES, especially through his 1936 book 'THE GENERAL THEORY of EMPLOYMENT, INTEREST and MONEY', written in the context of the Great Depression. Keynes emphasised aggregate demand and the role of government in managing the economy. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The historical event that gave a major impetus to the development of macroeconomics was the __________.
solution: The GREAT DEPRESSION of 1929–1933 — a period of mass UNEMPLOYMENT and collapse in output across capitalist economies — gave a MAJOR IMPETUS to the development of MACROECONOMICS. It exposed the limits of the classical view and led Keynes to develop new theories about aggregate demand and government intervention. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The FOUR major sectors (players) studied in macroeconomics are households, firms, government and __________.
options: The external sector (rest of the world)
solution: Macroeconomics studies FOUR major SECTORS or players: HOUSEHOLDS (consumers/owners of factors), FIRMS (producers), the GOVERNMENT (taxes, spending, policy), and the EXTERNAL SECTOR (the REST of the WORLD — exports, imports, capital flows). Their interactions determine the economy's performance. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In macroeconomics, households are primarily the __________.
options: Owners of factors of production and consumers of final goods and services
solution: In macroeconomics, HOUSEHOLDS are primarily the OWNERS of the FACTORS of PRODUCTION (land, labour, capital, enterprise) — which they supply to firms, earning income (rent, wages, interest, profit) — and the CONSUMERS of FINAL goods and services. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Firms in an economy are the units that __________.
options: Produce goods and services by employing/hiring the factors of production
solution: FIRMS are the PRODUCING units of the economy — they PRODUCE GOODS and SERVICES by EMPLOYING/HIRING the FACTORS of PRODUCTION (labour, land, capital) supplied by households, and they pay factor incomes in return. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A 'capitalist economy' is one in which __________.
options: The means of production are largely privately owned, and production is carried out for the market to earn profit, using hired labour
The state owns all means of production
There is no market or money
Goods are produced only for self-consumption
solution: A CAPITALIST ECONOMY is one in which the MEANS of PRODUCTION are largely PRIVATELY OWNED, production is carried out FOR the MARKET (for SALE) to EARN PROFIT, and there is widespread use of HIRED LABOUR (wage labour). Macroeconomics developed largely to analyse such economies. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'circular flow of income' shows __________.
options: The flow of goods/services and money (factor payments and consumption spending) between households and firms
The movement of only one product
solution: The CIRCULAR FLOW of INCOME shows the continuous FLOW of GOODS and SERVICES and of MONEY between the main sectors. In the simple version, HOUSEHOLDS supply factor services to FIRMS and receive FACTOR PAYMENTS (wages, rent, etc.); they spend this income buying goods/services from firms (CONSUMPTION spending), and the money flows back to firms — a never-ending circular flow. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In the simple circular flow model (two-sector economy), the two sectors are __________.
solution: In the SIMPLE (two-sector) CIRCULAR FLOW model, the two sectors are HOUSEHOLDS and FIRMS. Households provide factor services and consume goods; firms produce goods and pay factor incomes. (More complex models add the government and the external sector.) So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'real flow' in the circular flow of income refers to the flow of __________.
options: Goods, services and factor services between households and firms
solution: The REAL FLOW in the circular flow refers to the flow of GOODS, SERVICES, and FACTOR SERVICES — the flow of FACTOR SERVICES (labour, land, capital) from households to firms, and the flow of GOODS and SERVICES from firms to households. The MONEY FLOW (payments) moves in the opposite direction. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'money flow' (nominal flow) in the circular flow refers to __________.
options: The flow of factor payments (wages, rent, interest, profit) and consumption expenditure in monetary terms
solution: The MONEY FLOW (NOMINAL flow) refers to the flow of MONEY: FACTOR PAYMENTS (WAGES, RENT, INTEREST, PROFIT) from firms to households, and CONSUMPTION EXPENDITURE from households to firms. It runs OPPOSITE to the real flow of goods and services. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A 'stock' variable differs from a 'flow' variable in that a stock is measured __________.
options: At a point in time (e.g., capital, money supply), whereas a flow is measured over a period of time (e.g., income, investment)
Only over a period of time
solution: A STOCK variable is measured at a POINT in TIME (e.g., CAPITAL, WEALTH, MONEY SUPPLY on a given date, population at a moment). A FLOW variable is measured OVER a PERIOD of TIME (e.g., INCOME per year, INVESTMENT during a year, consumption per month). Distinguishing stocks from flows is important in macroeconomics. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following is a STOCK variable?
options: The quantity of capital (machines) in a factory on a given date
solution: The QUANTITY of CAPITAL (machines) in a factory ON a GIVEN DATE is a STOCK variable — measured at a point in time. National income (per year), monthly consumption, and annual investment are all FLOW variables, measured over a period. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Final goods' are those that __________.
options: Are used for final consumption or investment, not for further processing/resale within the year
Are used up entirely as inputs by other firms
solution: FINAL GOODS are goods that are used for FINAL CONSUMPTION (by consumers) or for INVESTMENT (capital formation) — they do NOT undergo any FURTHER PROCESSING or RESALE within the accounting year. They are counted in national income. This contrasts with intermediate goods. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Intermediate goods' are goods that __________.
options: Are used as raw materials or inputs in producing other goods, or are bought for resale within the year
Are bought by consumers for final use
solution: INTERMEDIATE GOODS are goods that are USED as RAW MATERIALS or INPUTS in the production of OTHER goods (e.g., raw cotton for cloth, flour for bread) or are BOUGHT for RESALE within the year. Their value is NOT counted separately in national income (to avoid double counting), as it is embodied in the value of final goods. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Final goods are further classified into consumption goods and __________ goods.
solution: FINAL GOODS are classified into CONSUMPTION GOODS (used to satisfy wants directly — food, clothes) and CAPITAL (INVESTMENT) GOODS (durable goods used to produce other goods — machines, tools, equipment). Capital goods add to the economy's productive capacity. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Consumption goods are further divided into durable, semi-durable, non-durable goods and __________.
solution: CONSUMPTION GOODS are divided into: DURABLE goods (long-lasting, like cars, TVs), SEMI-DURABLE goods (like clothes, crockery), NON-DURABLE goods (used up quickly, like food, fuel), and SERVICES (non-material, like teaching, transport, medical care). So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Capital goods' are distinguished by the fact that they __________.
options: Are durable goods used in the production process over several years (fixed assets like machinery, equipment)
Are always intermediate goods used up within a year
solution: CAPITAL GOODS are DURABLE goods used in the PRODUCTION PROCESS over SEVERAL YEARS — the FIXED ASSETS of firms, like MACHINERY, EQUIPMENT, tools, and buildings. They are not used up in a single year but gradually wear out (depreciation) while helping produce other goods. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Investment' in macroeconomics means __________.
options: The addition to the stock of capital goods (capital formation) in the economy during a period
Buying shares in the stock market
solution: In MACROECONOMICS, INVESTMENT means the ADDITION to the STOCK of CAPITAL GOODS — i.e., CAPITAL FORMATION — in the economy during a period (new machines, buildings, equipment, and additions to inventories). It is NOT the everyday sense of buying shares or saving; it refers to real additions to productive capacity. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Depreciation' (consumption of fixed capital) refers to __________.
options: The fall in the value of fixed capital assets due to normal wear and tear and expected obsolescence during use
solution: DEPRECIATION (CONSUMPTION of FIXED CAPITAL) refers to the FALL in the VALUE of FIXED CAPITAL ASSETS (machines, buildings) due to NORMAL WEAR and TEAR in the production process and EXPECTED OBSOLESCENCE over their working life. It represents the capital 'used up' in production. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Gross investment' minus depreciation equals __________.
solution: GROSS INVESTMENT is the TOTAL addition to capital stock before allowing for wear and tear. NET INVESTMENT = GROSS INVESTMENT − DEPRECIATION (consumption of fixed capital). Net investment shows the TRUE ADDITION to the productive capital stock after replacing worn-out capital. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The distinction between final and intermediate goods depends mainly on __________.
options: The end use of the good (who buys it and for what purpose), not on the nature of the good itself
solution: The distinction between FINAL and INTERMEDIATE goods depends mainly on the END USE of the good — WHO buys it and for WHAT PURPOSE — not on the physical nature of the good itself. For example, MILK bought by a household is a FINAL good, but milk bought by a sweet-shop to make sweets is an INTERMEDIATE good. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In a two-sector economy without government or foreign trade, in equilibrium the total production of firms equals __________.
options: The total consumption spending of households (which equals total income)
solution: In a simple TWO-SECTOR economy (households and firms) with NO government or foreign trade, and no saving/investment, in EQUILIBRIUM the TOTAL PRODUCTION of firms EQUALS the TOTAL CONSUMPTION SPENDING of households, which in turn equals the TOTAL INCOME (factor payments). Production = income = expenditure — the basis of the three methods of measuring national income. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following is an example of a service (rather than a good)?
options: The work of a doctor treating a patient
solution: A SERVICE is a non-material product that satisfies wants — for example, the WORK of a DOCTOR treating a patient (also teaching, transport, banking). A loaf of bread, a television, and a bag of wheat are all material GOODS. Both goods and services are counted in output. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'external sector' becomes important in an open economy because it involves __________.
options: Exports, imports and other transactions with the rest of the world
solution: The EXTERNAL SECTOR (rest of the world) is important in an OPEN ECONOMY because it involves EXPORTS (goods/services sold abroad), IMPORTS (bought from abroad), and other cross-border TRANSACTIONS (capital flows, remittances). These affect a country's income, employment, and balance of payments. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The government sector in macroeconomics affects the economy mainly through __________.
options: Taxation, public expenditure, and policies (fiscal and regulatory) that influence output and distribution
solution: The GOVERNMENT SECTOR affects the economy mainly through TAXATION (drawing income from households/firms), PUBLIC EXPENDITURE (spending on goods, services, and transfers), and POLICIES (FISCAL policy — taxing and spending — and regulation) that INFLUENCE aggregate OUTPUT, employment, prices, and the DISTRIBUTION of income. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): Intermediate goods are not counted separately in national income. Reason (R): Their value is already included in the value of the final goods they help produce, so counting them again would be double counting. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: A is TRUE — INTERMEDIATE GOODS are NOT counted separately in national income. R is TRUE and correctly EXPLAINS A: their VALUE is ALREADY INCLUDED in the VALUE of the FINAL GOODS they help produce, so counting them AGAIN would lead to DOUBLE COUNTING (overstating output). Hence only final goods (or value added) are counted. So R is the correct explanation of A. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following correctly matches a term with its meaning?
options: Stock → measured at a point in time; Flow → measured over a period; Final good → for final use; Intermediate good → input for further production
Stock → over a period; Flow → at a point; Final good → an input; Intermediate good → for final use
Stock and flow are identical; final and intermediate are identical
solution: The correct matches are: STOCK → measured at a POINT in TIME; FLOW → measured OVER a PERIOD of time; FINAL GOOD → for FINAL USE (consumption/investment); INTERMEDIATE GOOD → an INPUT used for FURTHER PRODUCTION or resale. So option 1 correctly pairs each term with its meaning. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A key assumption in the simple circular flow model is that __________.
options: Households spend their entire income on consumption (no saving), and firms sell all they produce, so there are no leakages
There is no spending at all
solution: A key ASSUMPTION in the SIMPLEST CIRCULAR FLOW model is that HOUSEHOLDS SPEND their ENTIRE INCOME on CONSUMPTION (there is NO SAVING) and FIRMS SELL all they produce, so there are NO LEAKAGES (like saving, taxes, or imports) and no injections. This keeps the flow constant and equal at every point (income = output = expenditure). So option 1 is correct.

stem: Why is macroeconomics important for policy-making?
options: It helps understand and manage economy-wide problems like unemployment, inflation, and slow growth through appropriate policies
It only helps price a single good
solution: MACROECONOMICS is important for POLICY-MAKING because it helps understand and MANAGE ECONOMY-WIDE PROBLEMS such as UNEMPLOYMENT, INFLATION (rising prices), recessions, and SLOW GROWTH. Governments and central banks use macroeconomic analysis to design FISCAL and MONETARY POLICIES that stabilise and grow the economy. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The classical economists (before Keynes) generally believed that a market economy __________.
options: Automatically tends toward full employment, so large-scale involuntary unemployment would not persist
Is always stuck in permanent depression
solution: The CLASSICAL ECONOMISTS believed that a MARKET ECONOMY AUTOMATICALLY TENDS toward FULL EMPLOYMENT of resources through flexible wages and prices, so LARGE-SCALE INVOLUNTARY UNEMPLOYMENT would NOT PERSIST. The Great Depression, with its mass, prolonged unemployment, challenged this view and led Keynes to develop macroeconomics. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Keynes argued that the level of employment and output in an economy is determined mainly by __________.
options: The size of the population alone
solution: KEYNES argued that the level of EMPLOYMENT and OUTPUT in an economy is determined mainly by AGGREGATE (EFFECTIVE) DEMAND — the total demand for goods and services in the economy. If aggregate demand is deficient, output and employment fall (unemployment); hence government can boost demand to raise employment. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In a purely capitalist economy, the central questions of what, how, and for whom to produce are decided mainly by __________.
options: The market mechanism (forces of demand and supply / the price system)
solution: In a purely CAPITALIST (market) economy, the central questions — WHAT to produce, HOW to produce, and FOR WHOM to produce — are decided mainly by the MARKET MECHANISM, i.e., the forces of DEMAND and SUPPLY working through the PRICE SYSTEM, with producers guided by profit. (In a planned economy, a central authority decides.) So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Wage labour' is a defining feature of capitalism, meaning that __________.
options: Workers sell their labour services to employers for a wage, rather than owning the means of production
No one is paid for work
solution: WAGE LABOUR is a defining feature of CAPITALISM: WORKERS SELL their LABOUR SERVICES to EMPLOYERS (capitalists) in exchange for a WAGE, rather than owning the means of production themselves. Production is organised by capitalists who hire this labour to produce for the market. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following is an INJECTION into the circular flow of income?
solution: INJECTIONS add to the circular flow of income: INVESTMENT, GOVERNMENT SPENDING, and EXPORTS. LEAKAGES (withdrawals) reduce it: SAVING, TAXES, and IMPORTS. In equilibrium, total injections equal total leakages. So investment is an injection. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following is a LEAKAGE (withdrawal) from the circular flow of income?
solution: LEAKAGES (WITHDRAWALS) from the circular flow reduce the flow of income: SAVING, TAXES, and IMPORTS. INVESTMENT, GOVERNMENT SPENDING, and EXPORTS are INJECTIONS that add to it. So saving is a leakage. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The value of output can be measured in three equivalent ways: as the value of production, as income, and as __________.
solution: The value of an economy's output can be measured in THREE EQUIVALENT ways, corresponding to the circular flow: the VALUE of PRODUCTION (product/value-added method), the total INCOME earned by factors (income method), and the total EXPENDITURE on final goods (expenditure method). Production = Income = Expenditure. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Inventory investment (change in stock of unsold goods and raw materials held by firms) is treated in national accounting as __________.
solution: INVENTORY INVESTMENT — the CHANGE in the STOCK of unsold finished goods, semi-finished goods, and raw materials held by firms — is treated as a PART of INVESTMENT (capital formation) in national accounting. An increase in inventories is positive investment; a decrease is negative. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A 'closed economy' is one that __________.
options: Does not engage in international trade (no exports or imports) with the rest of the world
solution: A CLOSED ECONOMY is one that does NOT engage in INTERNATIONAL TRADE — it has NO EXPORTS or IMPORTS and no economic transactions with the REST of the WORLD. An OPEN economy, by contrast, trades with other countries. The distinction affects how the circular flow and national income are modelled. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The main difference between a good and a service is that __________.
options: A good is a tangible/material product, while a service is intangible and consumed at the time it is produced
A service can be stored easily
solution: The main difference is that a GOOD is a TANGIBLE (material) product that can often be stored (e.g., a book, a car), while a SERVICE is INTANGIBLE and is generally CONSUMED at the TIME it is PRODUCED (e.g., a haircut, teaching, a bus ride) and cannot be stored. Both are counted in national output. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Machines bought by a firm to produce goods are classified as __________, whereas the same type of item bought by a household for personal use may be a consumer durable.
options: Intermediate goods used up within a year
solution: MACHINES bought by a FIRM to PRODUCE goods are classified as CAPITAL (INVESTMENT) GOODS — durable assets used in production over years. The classification depends on USE: a similar durable item bought by a HOUSEHOLD for personal use is a CONSUMER DURABLE. So for the firm's productive use, it is a capital good. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'four factors of production' whose owners receive incomes are land, labour, capital and __________.
solution: The FOUR FACTORS of PRODUCTION are LAND (earning RENT), LABOUR (earning WAGES), CAPITAL (earning INTEREST), and ENTREPRENEURSHIP/ENTERPRISE (earning PROFIT). Households own these factors and supply them to firms, receiving the corresponding factor incomes. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Households supplying factor services to firms receive rent, wages, interest and __________ as factor incomes.
solution: The FACTOR INCOMES received by households for supplying factor services are: RENT (for land), WAGES/salaries (for labour), INTEREST (for capital), and PROFIT (for entrepreneurship). Together these make up the income side of the circular flow. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Why can income, output, and expenditure be measured as equal in the economy?
options: Because every rupee of output produced is someone's income and is matched by expenditure on that output — they are three views of the same flow
Because the government sets them equal by law
solution: INCOME, OUTPUT, and EXPENDITURE are equal because they are THREE VIEWS of the SAME circular FLOW: every rupee of OUTPUT produced generates an equal amount of factor INCOME (payments to those who produced it), and that output is bought with an equal amount of EXPENDITURE. Hence Output = Income = Expenditure, which is why national income can be measured by any of the three methods. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A 'mixed economy' combines features of __________.
options: Both market (capitalist) and planned (government-directed) economies, with private and public sectors coexisting
solution: A MIXED ECONOMY combines features of BOTH the MARKET (CAPITALIST) economy and the PLANNED (government-directed) economy — the PRIVATE SECTOR and the PUBLIC SECTOR COEXIST, with markets allocating many resources while the government also plans, regulates, and provides certain goods and services. India is an example of a mixed economy. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The purchase of a second-hand (used) good, like an old car, is NOT included in this year's national income because __________.
options: It was already counted when it was originally produced; only its production, not its resale, adds to output
solution: The purchase of a SECOND-HAND (used) good is NOT included in this year's national income because it was ALREADY COUNTED when it was originally PRODUCED (in an earlier year). National income measures CURRENT PRODUCTION; a mere RESALE of an existing good transfers ownership but adds NO new output. (Any commission to a dealer, being a current service, would be counted.) So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following pairs correctly identifies injections and leakages?
options: Injections: investment, government spending, exports; Leakages: saving, taxes, imports
Injections: saving, taxes, imports; Leakages: investment, exports
Injections and leakages are the same thing
There are no injections in any economy
solution: The correct identification is: INJECTIONS (adding to the circular flow) are INVESTMENT, GOVERNMENT SPENDING, and EXPORTS; LEAKAGES (withdrawals from the flow) are SAVING, TAXES, and IMPORTS. In macroeconomic equilibrium, total injections equal total leakages. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The study of how the general price level and total employment are determined is a concern of __________.
solution: The determination of the GENERAL PRICE LEVEL (inflation/deflation) and TOTAL (aggregate) EMPLOYMENT in the whole economy is a central concern of MACROECONOMICS. Microeconomics instead studies the prices of individual goods and the allocation of resources among particular uses. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Introduction' (to macroeconomics) is that:
options: MACROECONOMICS studies the ECONOMY as a WHOLE — aggregates like national income, output, employment and the price level — as distinct from MICROECONOMICS (individual units); it emerged largely with KEYNES after the GREAT DEPRESSION; the economy has four key sectors — HOUSEHOLDS, FIRMS, GOVERNMENT and the EXTERNAL SECTOR — whose interactions are shown by the CIRCULAR FLOW of income (real and money flows between households and firms); and it rests on basic concepts such as STOCK vs FLOW variables, FINAL vs INTERMEDIATE goods, CONSUMPTION and CAPITAL goods, INVESTMENT and DEPRECIATION — providing the foundation for measuring national income and managing the economy
The Great Depression had no effect on economics
solution: The chapter's overall message is that MACROECONOMICS studies the ECONOMY as a WHOLE — analysing AGGREGATES like NATIONAL INCOME, total OUTPUT, EMPLOYMENT, and the general PRICE LEVEL — as distinct from MICROECONOMICS, which studies INDIVIDUAL units (a consumer, firm, or single market). It EMERGED as a distinct branch largely with J.M. KEYNES following the GREAT DEPRESSION of the 1930s. The economy is analysed through FOUR key SECTORS — HOUSEHOLDS (consumers/factor owners), FIRMS (producers), the GOVERNMENT (taxes and spending), and the EXTERNAL SECTOR (rest of the world) — whose interactions are captured by the CIRCULAR FLOW of INCOME, with a REAL FLOW of goods/factor services and an opposite MONEY FLOW between households and firms. It rests on basic CONCEPTS: STOCK versus FLOW variables, FINAL versus INTERMEDIATE goods, CONSUMPTION versus CAPITAL goods, and INVESTMENT and DEPRECIATION — all of which provide the FOUNDATION for measuring national income and understanding and managing the economy. So the overall message is option 2.
